title: STELLAR: Storage Tuning Engine Leveraging LLM Autonomous Reasoning for High Performance Parallel File Systems
problem: Tuning parallel file systems (HPC I/O) is complex and manpower-intensive, requiring deep expertise. Current autotuning methods require hundreds of thousands of iterations, making optimization inaccessible to most scientists.
motivation: I/O performance is crucial for data-intensive HPC but tuning large-scale storage systems is costly and difficult. Traditional autotuning approaches converge slowly. LLM-powered autonomous tuning could accelerate this process.
method: STELLAR uses an LLM (a large language model that acts as an autonomous reasoning system) to automatically tune parallel file systems. It starts by extracting tunable parameters from system manuals and analyzing I/O traces (recordings of how data moves through the system), then proposes tuning strategies and runs test applications to measure their effectiveness. Based on the results, it refines its strategies and learns from each attempt. The system combines retrieval-augmented generation (looking up specific parameter knowledge when reasoning), tool execution, LLM-based reasoning, and a multiagent design (multiple specialized agents that work together and verify each other's thinking).
key_novelty: STELLAR introduces LLM-based autonomous reasoning to automatically tune parallel file systems, combining multiagent design to make the reasoning more reliable and retrieval-augmented generation to access parameter knowledge from documentation.
contributions: STELLAR autonomous tuner powered by LLMs
Near-optimal configuration selection within first five attempts
Human-like efficiency (vs hundreds of thousands of iterations for traditional autotuning)
RAG integration for parameter extraction from manuals
External tool execution and closed-loop tuning

metrics.iterations_to_optimality: ~5 attempts (vs hundreds of thousands for traditional autotuning)

limitations: LLM hallucinations require multiagent mitigation; may not work for all file system types; requires representative workloads for profiling.
